theme: How lovely is your dwelling place
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 84. It is a pilgrim’s song, a longing for the courts of the LORD. Read it slowly and notice the happy people it describes.
settingTheScene: Psalm 84 is a psalm of the sons of Korah, who were temple singers and doorkeepers. It is a song for pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem for one of the feasts, probably Tabernacles. It is among the most beloved psalms of all time. Following the dedication of the temple and the song of Zion, it expresses the deep desire of the heart to be where God is.
observation: “How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!” (v. 1).
“My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God” (v. 2).
“Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars” (v. 3).
“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise!” (v. 4).
“Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion” (v. 5).
“As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs” (v. 6).
“For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness” (v. 10).
“For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly” (v. 11).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with exclamation. “How lovely!” It is not a calm analysis but an outburst of longing. The poet’s soul “faints” for the temple. “My heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.” Worship is not merely duty. It is joy and desire. The psalm teaches us to want what we ought to want.

The sparrow and the swallow are a charming picture. Even the smallest birds make their homes near the altar. The poet envies them. They live in the presence of God. It is an image of belonging: the smallest and least can find a home in God’s house.

Then come two beatitudes. First, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” Second, “Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion.” The second is subtle. The pilgrim has the roads to Zion in his heart. Even when he is far away, his heart is already traveling. A heart set on pilgrimage makes the journey a blessing.

“As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs.” Baca means “weeping.” The pilgrim route passes through a dry valley, a place of sorrow. But those who go with their hearts set on God transform the valley into springs. Suffering becomes a source of refreshment. And “they go from strength to strength.” The pilgrimage is a journey in which strength grows.

The famous tenth verse puts it simply: “A day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere.” The poet would rather be a doorkeeper, the lowest servant, at God’s house than live in luxury elsewhere. Being near God is the greatest good. The psalm ends with a promise: “No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly.”
connection: Jesus is the sun and shield, and the true dwelling place (John 1:14; Malachi 4:2). He said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28). In him, believers have access to the Father (Ephesians 2:18; Hebrews 10:19-22). Romans 8:32 echoes verse 11: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” Philippians 3:8-14 shows Paul pressing on to know Christ.
application:
Ask whether you long for God’s presence. If not, ask him to give you the desire.

When you walk through your own “Valley of Baca,” consider how God may turn it into springs.

Meet with God’s people this week, and treat it as a gift.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what your soul longs for.
Ask him to make your strength be in him.
Say aloud that a day in his courts is better than a thousand elsewhere.
